summary: Describes source-specific multicast for IP. IPv4 addresses in 232/8 and IPv6 addresses with the FF3x::/32 prefix are reserved for SSM, where receivers ask for traffic from a particular source to a group address. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Source-Specific Multicast lets a receiver request traffic from one named sender to a multicast address. Routers use that request to forward only the selected source's traffic.

subtitle: Multicast delivery where receivers identify both the sender and the destination group.

tldr.problem: In ordinary multicast, a receiver joins a group without naming a sender, so traffic from different sources can share that group.
tldr.mechanism: Source-Specific Multicast identifies a channel by source S and group G. Hosts subscribe to that pair, and routers forward only when a receiver has requested it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4607 reserves IPv4 232/8 and IPv6 FF3x::/32 for this service and specifies host and router behavior. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

facts.label: Host membership protocols
facts.value: IGMPv3 for IPv4; MLDv2 for IPv6

today: RFC 4607 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multicast Names a Source
sections.content:
Ordinary any-source multicast delivers traffic sent to a group address G to hosts that joined G. RFC 4607 defines a different service, Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), in which the sender's address is part of the delivery request.

This model avoids cross-delivery when different senders use the same destination address. It also avoids the need for receivers to coordinate destination choices. SSM suits applications whose senders are known before the application begins, but it does not directly provide network-layer service discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary multicast asks for all traffic to a group. SSM asks for traffic to that group from one particular sender.

sections.title: A Channel Is a Source and a Group
sections.content:
An SSM channel is the pair (S,G): source address S and multicast destination G. A host subscribes to that pair and receives matching datagrams. Two sources using the same G are different channels.

For ordinary multicast, the RFC uses the term host group and the operations Join(G) and Leave(G). For SSM, it uses channel and Subscribe(S,G) or Unsubscribe(S,G). A request that names G but omits S is invalid for SSM and routers must ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: A channel includes the sender's address and the group's address. Naming only the group does not tell an SSM router which traffic the receiver wants.

sections.title: Reserved SSM Address Ranges
sections.content:
IPv4 SSM uses the address range 232/8, from 232.0.0.0 through 232.255.255.255. IPv6 SSM uses the prefix FF3x::/32, where x is a valid scope identifier.

The addresses 232.0.0.0 and FF3x::4000:0000 are reserved and must not be used as destinations. IANA allocates specified subranges; other allowed addresses are selected locally by sending hosts. A host must not allocate addresses sequentially from the first allowed value. Random selection is recommended to reduce collisions on shared links.
sections.plainLanguage: SSM has dedicated IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges. Hosts select addresses locally, and the RFC recommends random selection rather than counting upward from the start.

sections.title: Host and Router Responsibilities
sections.content:
A host's IP module sends a subscription when its first socket requests a channel on an interface, and sends an unsubscription when the last socket leaves. IPv4 hosts use IGMPv3 and IPv6 hosts use MLDv2 for these requests. The IP module must deliver a datagram only to sockets whose source, group and interface match.

A router silently drops an SSM datagram unless a neighboring host or router has requested that source and destination. Supporting routers implement the PIM-SSM subset of PIM-SM and the router portions of IGMPv3 and MLDv2. A router must not create forwarding state from a request that names only a group.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts tell routers which sender and group they want. Routers forward matching traffic and discard SSM traffic that nobody requested.

sections.title: Security, Transition and Address Allocation
sections.content:
SSM does not authenticate a packet's source by itself. An attacker can forge a source address and send traffic on another sender's channel, so applications that need strong authentication must use a higher-layer mechanism. The RFC also describes denial-of-service risk from excessive subscriptions and allows routers to limit subscription rates or counts.

Routers must ignore older group-only reports for SSM addresses rather than treating them as requests for every source. IANA can allocate well-known SSM addresses from designated ranges, but must not assign the rest to specific entities or applications.
sections.plainLanguage: SSM chooses traffic by source address but does not prove that the sender owns that address. Applications needing proof must add authentication, and routers can limit subscription requests.
